column3: It repeats the whole-earth-plus-its-like ransom scenario and explicitly says it will not be accepted on the Day of Resurrection.
The immediately preceding prayer names God as knower of unseen and seen and judge of disputed matters, framing the disclosure in the focus.
Professing to hear while not hearing does not clarify ransom, resurrection judgment, or unexpected disclosure.
It closely repeats the impossible whole-earth-plus-its-like ransom and connects it to a terrible reckoning.
The immediate sequel makes their evil earnings visible and lets the mocked reality close around them, directly extending the focus's disclosure.
The certain day when God gathers all people supplies the judicial setting for the focus's failed ransom.
It states that every wrongdoing soul would ransom itself with all the earth on seeing punishment, followed by just judgment.
Its near-identical disclosure of evil deeds and the engulfing mocked consequence closely parallels the focus's next-stage outcome.
It denies that the wrongdoers are overlooked and defers them to a terrifying day, supporting the focus's delayed judgment.
The same-surah warning makes wrongdoers face the evil punishment on Resurrection Day and taste what they earned.
The human's claim to possess blessing through knowledge illustrates the false private calculation overturned by the focus's unforeseen disclosure.
God's unbroken promise and vengeance explain why the awaited judgment in the focus cannot be escaped.
Its Resurrection-Day vision of the earth entirely in God's grasp relativizes the immense possession imagined as a ransom in the focus.
The immediate continuation says former people's earnings did not avail them, confirming that acquired resources cannot avert consequence.
It identifies denial of signs as self-wronging, a general moral condition behind the focus's judgment.
Wrongdoers see punishment and then recognize that all power belongs to God, an eschatological unveiling related to the focus.
Re-creation from the creation of heaven and earth does not specifically clarify ransom or unforeseen judgment.
The challenge to produce a likeness of the Qur'an does not illuminate the focus's judgment scene.
The reversal of worldly mockery on Resurrection Day gives only a broad eschatological contrast.
The immediate continuation says the evil results of their earnings will strike the wrongdoers and that they cannot frustrate it.
The creative command concerns divine origination, not the focus's ransom or disclosure.
It explicitly rejects an earth-full ransom of gold from those who die in disbelief and assigns painful punishment.
The same-surah contrast between worldly disgrace and the greater punishment of the Hereafter reinforces the focus's final consequence.
God's knowledge of what people reveal and conceal loosely supports the eventual exposure in the focus.
The condemned cannot escape in the earth or find protectors apart from God, explaining why material ransom cannot secure them.
The evil punishment closes around Pharaoh's people while a believer is protected, paralleling the focus's engulfing consequence.
It directly declares that no ransom will be taken that day and assigns the Fire as the destination.
It associates wrongdoers with the punishment of a painful day, supplying a compact judgment parallel.
The same-surah precedent says punishment came to earlier deniers from where they did not perceive, closely matching the focus's unanticipated outcome.
Its exact proportion between evil deed and recompense grounds the focus's treatment of wrongdoing as personally answerable.
It links evil punishment to a continuing judgment reaching Resurrection Day, extending the focus's punishment theme.
Nothing hidden in heaven or earth escapes the clear record, supporting the focus's eventual emergence of uncounted realities.
The appearance of Adam and Eve's nakedness after disobedience is a distant instance of concealed consequence becoming visible.
Universal belief by divine will does not clarify ransom, judgment, or unforeseen disclosure.
The same-surah judgment scene repays every soul in full for what it did, directly supplying the focus's accounting principle.
The comparison of Jesus and Adam concerns creation, not the focus's eschatological reckoning.
The criminal's wish to ransom himself from that day's punishment with his children extends the focus's futile-ransom image.
It gives evil earners a matching recompense, humiliation, and no protector from God, clarifying the judgment the focus anticipates.
Bearing sin and becoming companions of the Fire gives a general consequence for wrongdoing without the focus's ransom scene.
Wrongdoers have an allotted share like those before them and should not hasten it, reinforcing an unavoidable appointed consequence.
Its unmeasured reward for the patient is only a broad contrast to the wrongdoers' failed calculation.
The mistaken appearance of the sleepers offers a remote perception-versus-reality parallel.
Those who break God's covenant and spread corruption receive curse and the evil abode, naming conduct that leads to punitive outcome.
It makes each bearer responsible for no other burden and promises return and report of deeds, directly grounding the focus's nontransferable liability.
The contrast of darkness and light does not clarify the focus's judgment scene.
Permission to resist oppression concerns worldly redress rather than the focus's final punishment.
Matters disclosed to people that cause distress loosely echo disclosure, but in a different legal setting.
Their failure to expect any reckoning directly explains the focus's reference to what they did not take into account.
A mistaken estimate about military factions does not illuminate the eschatological calculation in the focus.
A prior community's questioning and disbelief do not clarify ransom or final disclosure.
Fabricating against God or denying His signs identifies grave wrongdoing but adds no specific judgment mechanism.
Hardening after a long interval concerns receptivity to revelation, not the focus's final exposure.
The confirmation that the threatened matter is true and cannot be escaped supports the certainty of the focus's punishment.
God's power to gather all creatures supports the Resurrection-Day assembly presupposed by the focus.
A cry seizes wrongdoers in a historical punishment, a general but non-eschatological consequence parallel.
God's ownership of all heaven and earth and the truth of His promise undercut the imagined efficacy of possessing the earth as ransom.
Divine forgiveness and mercy are better than what people accumulate, directly relativizing gathered material wealth.
The excellence of creation does not clarify the focus's accounting or ransom.
The admission that people do not guard the unseen offers only a loose contrast to the unforeseen reality in the focus.
The ruined man has no party to help him apart from God and cannot defend himself, reinforcing the failure of other securities.
Abraham says he possesses no power for another before God, supporting the focus's denial that any external resource can avert divine judgment.
Earlier people taste the consequence of their affair and receive painful punishment, providing a broad precedent for retributive outcome.
The question about punishment and warnings is too general to clarify the focus's ransom or disclosure.
The parable of divine light does not illuminate the focus's judicial scene.
The speakers acknowledge that they did not guard the unseen, a remote resonance with the focus's unanticipated disclosure.
Questioning whether the sleepers were wondrous signs gives only a broad challenge to human expectation.
Marriage provision and divine abundance do not clarify the focus.
Public and hidden speech about evil offers only a limited reveal-and-conceal parallel.
The confession of having been wrongdoers reflects recognition of guilt without the focus's ransom or Day of Resurrection.
Revealing or concealing good and pardoning evil gives a lexical disclosure parallel in a different ethical context.
The accusation against Mary does not clarify the focus's themes.
Everything in heaven and earth is subjected by God, reinforcing that the whole earth cannot function independently as a ransom.
Mockery and refusal to repent are called wrongdoing, but the verse does not develop final judgment.
Pharaoh's drowning with his followers does not clarify the focus's eschatological ransom.
The promised Hell directly supplies the destination implied by the focus's evil punishment.
The warning against assuming entry into Paradise without trial is a distant correction of false expectation.
The incomplete statement does not provide a meaningful connection to the focus.
It explicitly assigns the final reckoning to God, directly grounding the focus's account and judgment.
Clear verses bringing people from darkness to light offer a broad contrast to those surprised by final reality.
Disbelievers continue to receive calamity until God's promise arrives, linking their deeds to an unavoidable promised outcome.
The decree to fill Hell with Iblis and his followers supplies the punitive endpoint for those who follow wrongdoing.
It explicitly multiplies punishment on the Day of Resurrection and fixes humiliating permanence there.
Their denial of resurrection identifies the false expectation that the focus overturns at the Day of Judgment.
Those who think withheld wealth is good find it turned into a burden on Resurrection Day, closely exemplifying an unexpected reversal of property.
The wrongdoers are told they will learn who receives the final outcome, anticipating the focus's exposure of what they had not reckoned with.
Though punishment is delayed, an appointed time remains and no refuge exists apart from God, explaining why escape through ransom fails.
The creative command concerns divine power but not the focus's judgment themes.
Worldly spending is destroyed like a crop because people wrong themselves, showing that accumulated resources can fail through wrongdoing.
Jonah's prior glorification does not clarify the focus.
God owns all heaven and earth and will certainly gather humanity for Resurrection Day, directly framing the focus's imagined ransom and judgment.
Divine names and universal praise do not clarify the focus's ransom or disclosure.
The challenge to produce a surah does not illuminate the focus's final accounting.
The challenge to produce comparable speech does not clarify the focus.
The apparently fixed mountains moving like clouds gives a distant image of reality proving other than human estimation.
The declaration of collective caution does not clarify the focus.
God does not destroy towns while their people are unaware, supplying a justice condition relevant to the focus's unanticipated judgment.
Rules for safeguarding orphan property do not clarify the focus's eschatological themes.
Wrongdoers alter the commanded word and receive punishment because of their wrongdoing, a historical retribution parallel.
Creation in truth and the return to God provide a broad framework for the final accountability in the focus.
The sky's rupture is an eschatological sign, but it does not clarify failed ransom or unforeseen disclosure.
It explicitly says that no compensation will be accepted from a soul on the Day when no soul can avail another.
It repeats the warning that no ransom, intercession, or help will be accepted on the day of individual accountability.
The coming day without trade, friendship, or intercession supports the focus's denial that worldly assets can avert judgment.
Every soul finds its good and evil deeds made present, directly developing the focus's unforeseen appearance of what was excluded from calculation.
Whoever commits evil is repaid for it and finds no protector or helper apart from God, reinforcing personal liability.
What they had concealed before becomes manifest to them, a direct disclosure parallel to the focus's bada lahum.
Those who deny the meeting with God are overtaken by the Hour suddenly, illustrating a ruinous event arriving outside their expectation.
Even if a soul offers every ransom, it will not be accepted, directly reinforcing the focus's failed attempt to ransom oneself.
The weighing of deeds on that day supplies the evaluative mechanism that makes material substitution impossible.
Punishment seizes people suddenly while they are unaware, closely related to the focus's unanticipated outcome.
Each soul tests what it previously sent ahead and returns to God, while its fabricated assumptions vanish.
All people come forth before God and the weak discover that their former leaders cannot avail them, a direct final-exposure scene.
The transformation of earth and heavens on the day people emerge before the One God expands the setting of the focus's Day of Resurrection.
Every soul comes pleading for itself and is repaid in full for what it did, directly grounding the focus's personal reckoning.
Each person's record is bound to them and will be produced openly on Resurrection Day.
The command to read one's own record makes the hidden moral account visible and self-evidencing.
God gathers all people on the day the earth is exposed and leaves none of them behind, supplying the focus's universal judgment setting.
The opened record leaves out no small or great deed and makes people fear what is set before them, closely paralleling unforeseen disclosure.
Every person comes to God alone on Resurrection Day, excluding the force of wealth, allies, or transferable support.
Faces are humbled before the Living Sustainer, and the wrongdoer fails, giving the focus's punishment scene an immediate posture of defeat.
The scales of justice on Resurrection Day weigh even a mustard seed and ensure no soul is wronged.
When the trumpet is blown, family relations and mutual inquiries cease, strengthening the focus's picture of irreducible individual exposure.
On the day wealth and children do not avail, only a sound heart benefits, directly countering the imagined efficacy of material ransom.
Wrongdoers despair when the Hour arrives, portraying the collapse of prior expectation at final judgment.
A barrier is placed between people and what they desire, as with earlier counterparts who had been in unsettling doubt.
The trumpet summons people from graves to their Lord, directly supplying the resurrection scene assumed by the focus.
No soul is wronged that day and each is repaid only for what it did, directly confirming nontransferable retribution.
The condemned are halted because they are to be questioned, an immediate accounting image for the focus's judgment.
The trumpet brings death and then resurrection, supplying the same-surah transition into the final Day presupposed by the focus.
The earth is illuminated, the record and witnesses are brought, and judgment is rendered without injustice, expanding the focus's disclosure into its full courtroom scene.
On the day people come forth, nothing concerning them is concealed from God, directly parallel to the focus's emergence of the unreckoned.
The wrongdoers' excuses do not benefit them on the day they are judged, confirming that later defenses cannot offset their consequence.
Wrongdoers see the Fire with humiliation and believers identify the real loss as losing oneself and one's family on Resurrection Day.
On the Day of Decision no protector can avail another, directly reinforcing the focus's failed search for relief from punishment.
God created in truth so that every soul may be repaid for what it earned without injustice, matching the focus's retributive logic.
Every community is summoned to its record and told it will be repaid for what it did, directly developing the focus's account made visible.
The trumpet comes with the true event, marking the arrival of the promised Day that overturns prior calculation.
The covering is removed and sight becomes sharp, a direct image of reality becoming visible after being disregarded.
No bearer bears another's burden, reinforcing why each wrongdoer must face a liability that cannot be shifted or bought off.
God raises all people and informs them of what they did; they forgot their deeds while God had counted them all.
God comes upon them from where they did not expect, giving a close lexical and thematic parallel to unanticipated divine action.
The Day of Gathering is named the day of mutual loss and gain, supplying the collective final setting for the focus.
God provides from where a person does not expect, a deliberate positive counterpart to the focus's unexpected divine disclosure to wrongdoers.
On the Day of Exposure no secret is hidden, directly expressing the disclosure element of the focus.
No intimate friend asks about another on that day, reinforcing the isolation of the person seeking ransom in the focus.
The wrongdoer wishes to ransom himself from that day's punishment with his spouse and brother, extending the focus's futile-ransom sequence.
He would offer his nearest family who shelters him, further specifying the desperate but ineffective substitutes for himself.
He would offer everyone on earth to save himself, directly matching the focus's whole-earth ransom image.
Every soul is held in pledge for what it earned, concisely grounding the focus's personal moral liability.
No soul can avail another on that day, and all command belongs to God, directly undercutting every imagined means of ransom.
Receiving one's record in the right hand introduces the public accounting structure behind the focus's judgment.
Receiving one's record behind the back gives the contrasting condemned form of that same disclosed account.
All people return to God before the accounting stated in the next ayah, completing the focus's final-return setting.
Whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, making deeds visible at the final reckoning.
Whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it, directly developing the focus's exposure of consequences that were not counted on.
